newsitem.title: FRANCE: New spy charge against late French defence chief.
newsitem.headline: New spy charge against late French defence chief.

text.p: A French magazine published fresh documents on Thursday purported to show that the late French Socialist defence minister Charles Hernu spied for the communist bloc in the 1950s and 1960s.

The weekly L'Express published the translation of a document which it said was addressed by the Soviet KGB intelligence service to Romanian services in 1963 saying Hernu, under the codename "Andre", had been a Soviet and Bulgarian agent for a decade.
Hernu, defence minister from 1981 to 1985, died in 1990.

Hernu's son Patrice, who sought but failed to obtain a judge's order to stop the magazine going on sale, denied the spying allegations. L'Express first alleged Hernu had been an east bloc agent last November.
"The elements provided have already been cited and the analysis shows they are a manipulation," he told France 2 television.
His lawyer Serge Lewisch, disputing their authenticity, told Reuters he would ask L'Express to produce the original documents to check their content and the translation.
He said a Paris court would hear next Wednesday his plea disputing the allegations made in November as well as the new charges. French media have widely reported the charges against Hernu.
L'Express said the purported KGB document had been intended to warn Romania not to recruit Hernu for its own secret services.

The document said "Andre" had accepted weekly payments from Bulgarian services from 1954 to 1956 while insisting he was giving information not for money but because of his political beliefs and on condition it did not harm France's interests.
The document said control of "Andre" was transferred to a Soviet spymaster in 1957. L'Express said it was not clear if Hernu had maintained relations with Soviet services after 1963.

In other documents dated 1957-58 and purported to come from the archives of the Soviet Foreign Ministry, a diplomat named as Vladimir Yerofeyev and former Soviet ambassador to France Sergei Vinogradov recounted lunch conversations with Hernu in memoranda addressed directly to foreign minister Andrei Gromyko.

L'Express said Hernu had disclosed the address of U.S. secret services in Paris and the number of French troops fighting Algerian pro-independence rebels and had given analyses and forecasts of French politics.

Hernu's family filed legal action for slander against L'Express last November. Patrice Hernu met a senior aide to President Jacques Chirac and said the talks reinforced his belief that the report was wrong.

L'Express said in November that France's DST counter-intelligence service had informed the late president Francois Mitterrand, Hernu's political patron, in 1992 after it received a dossier from east European spy services.
It said the DST had been unable to verify the charges and Mitterrand had ordered the reports to be kept secret, arguing Hernu could not defend himself.
